**Given:** The hypotheses and conventions stated in the formulation.

[A1] For each nonempty interval, an affine rescaling of $b(s)=\exp(-1/(1-s^2))$ for $|s|<1$, extended by zero, is a positive smooth compactly supported bump; its integral is positive and finite, so it can be normalized to one.

[F1] [[thm-continuous-on-a-rectangle-is-riemann-integrable]]: a continuous real function on a closed nondegenerate finite-dimensional rectangle is Riemann integrable.

[F2] [[thm-riemann-fubini-on-product-rectangles]]: if a Riemann-integrable function on a product of closed rectangles has integrable sections, its ordinary iterated integrals in both orders exist and equal its multiple integral.

[F3] [[thm-differentiation-under-the-integral-sign-on-a-compact-rectangle]]: for continuous real $g$ and its continuous parameter derivative on a compact two-variable rectangle, that derivative passes through the finite integral, including one-sided parameter endpoints.

[F4] [[lem-uniform-integral-error-bound]]: if integrable $f,g$ differ in sup norm by at most $M$ on $[a,b]$, their integrals differ by at most $(b-a)M$.

[F5] [[thm-holder-inequality-for-integrals]]: for real square-integrable functions, $\int|fg|\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2$; in particular, on an interval of length $\ell$, $|\int g|^2\le\ell\int|g|^2$.



**Given:** A nonempty finite rectangle $\Omega$, the test-space seminorms in the Statement, and a zero-integral test $h$.

1.1 For the given rectangle, fix once for all inputs and support sets an affine copy of the bump in [A1] on each side interval. Every derivative on $|s|<1$ is the exponential times a finite sum of rational terms with poles of finite order at $|s|=1$; $e^{-1/(1-s^2)}$ tends to zero faster than every such power, so extension by zero is smooth. By [F1] its continuous compact-interval integral exists; positivity makes it nonzero, so normalization gives $\theta_i$. For $d=1$, put $(Rh)(x)=\int_{a_1}^x h(s)\,ds$. The primitive difference quotient differs from $h(x)$ by at most $\sup\{|h(s)-h(x)|:s\text{ lies between }x\text{ and }x+\delta\}$, which tends to zero by continuity. Its derivative is therefore $h$, and it vanishes near both endpoints because $h$ is compactly supported and has total integral zero. Its support is compact inside the interval, and its $j$th derivative is $h^{(j-1)}$ for $j\ge1$; the zeroth seminorm is bounded by $(b_1-a_1)\sup|h|$. [given, A1, F1, F4, algebra]

1.2 Here and below the coordinate integrals of smooth compactly supported functions may be computed on the closed coordinate intervals after extension by zero. This extension is smooth on a neighborhood of the closed box: compact support leaves a neighborhood of every boundary face where the function is zero. By [F1] the function and every coordinate section are Riemann integrable; [F2], applied to successive coordinate blocks, identifies all iterated orders with the same box integral. In particular, the marginal $H(x')=\int_{a_1}^{b_1}h(s,x')\,ds$ has total integral equal to $\int_\Omega h$. [given, F1, F2]

1.3 To differentiate a marginal, fix all other coordinates and restrict the differentiated coordinate to a compact interval inside its open side interval. The integrand and each parameter derivative are continuous on the resulting compact two-variable rectangle, so repeated [F3] gives $$\partial_{x'}^\beta H(x')=\int_{a_1}^{b_1}\partial_{x'}^\beta h(s,x')\,ds,\qquad \sup|\partial^\beta H|\le (b_1-a_1)\sup|\partial_{x'}^\beta h|.$$ The inequality follows from [F4] with the second integrand zero. Continuity of these derivatives jointly in the remaining parameters follows from the same bound applied to their differences and uniform continuity of the integrand derivative on each compact box. [given, F3, F4]

1.4 We now prove the additional estimate for the very same fixed-bump map constructed in steps 1.1 and 3.1. Put $\ell=b_1-a_1$ and, for a smooth $g$ on the box, $Jg(x_1,x')=\int_{a_1}^{x_1}g(s,x')\,ds$. By [F5], $|Jg(x_1,x')|^2\le\ell\int_{a_1}^{b_1}|g(s,x')|^2\,ds$; integration over $x_1$ and $x'$ gives $\|Jg\|_2\le\ell\|g\|_2$. The smooth derivative identities in steps 1.3–2.1 give $\partial_1Jg=g$ and $\partial_jJg=J(\partial_jg)$ for $j>1$, so

2.1 The same reasoning differentiates an integral with upper endpoint $x_1$ in its other parameters. For its $x_1$ derivative, the difference quotient of $\int_{a_1}^{x_1}f(s,x')\,ds$ differs from $f(x_1,x')$ by at most $\sup_{s\text{ between }x_1\text{ and }x_1+\delta}|f(s,x')-f(x_1,x')|$, which tends to zero by continuity; higher endpoint derivatives then follow by ordinary differentiation. This proves the finite-integral identities used in the recursion. [given, F3, F4, step 1.3]

3.1 For $d>1$, let $x'=(x_2,\ldots,x_d)$ and $H(x')=\int_{a_1}^{b_1}h(s,x')\,ds$. By step 1.2, $\int H=\int h=0$, and steps 1.3–2.1 show that $H$ and the displayed primitives are smooth. Assuming the construction in dimension $d-1$, define $$(Rh)_1=\int_{a_1}^{x_1}\bigl(h(s,x')-\theta_1(s)H(x')\bigr)\,ds,\qquad (Rh)_j=\theta_1(x_1)(R'H)_{j-1}(x')\quad(j\ge2).$$ Differentiating gives $\operatorname{div}(Rh)=h-\theta_1H+\theta_1H=h$. The first component vanishes both before the support and after its total first-coordinate integral, which is zero; the other components are compactly supported by induction. [given, A1, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 1.3, step 2.1, induction]

4.1 If inputs are supported in fixed compact $K$, each coordinate projection $K_i$ is compactly contained in $(a_i,b_i)$. Choose closed intervals $J_i\Subset(a_i,b_i)$ containing $K_i$ and the support of the already fixed bump $\theta_i$. Their product is a common compact output-support set $K'=\prod_iJ_i$: before the first-coordinate support the primitive is zero, and after it the primitive is zero because its full first-coordinate integral is zero; the other components have the required support by induction. [given, A1, step 1.1, step 3.1, induction]


5.1 Write $p_m(f)=\max_{|\alpha|\le m}\sup|\partial^\alpha f|$, taking the maximum also over components for vector fields, and put $\ell_1=b_1-a_1$. Step 1.3 gives $p_m(H)\le\ell_1p_m(h)$. For the first component in step 3.1, a derivative with no $x_1$ differentiation is an integral of $\partial_{x'}^\beta h-\theta_1\partial_{x'}^\beta H$ and is bounded by $\ell_1(1+\ell_1\|\theta_1\|_\infty)p_m(h)$. If the derivative differentiates $x_1$ at least once, the endpoint identity in step 2.1 gives a derivative of $h$ minus a fixed derivative of $\theta_1$ times a derivative of $H$, again bounded by a constant times $p_m(h)$. For each remaining component $\theta_1(x_1)(R'H)_{j-1}(x')$, the product derivative is bounded by a fixed bump-derivative constant times $p_m(R'H)\le C'_m p_m(H)$ by induction. The dimension-one bounds in step 1.1 start this induction. Thus $$p_m(Rh)\le C_m p_m(h)\qquad(m\ge0),$$ where $C_m$ depends only on the fixed rectangle, bumps, dimension and $m$, not on $h$. These are all fixed-support seminorm estimates, proving the full stated continuity. Every displayed construction is linear in $h$, and the bumps were fixed once independently of $h$ and $K$, so the same map $R$ serves all compact input supports. [given, A1, F4, step 1.1, step 1.3, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, induction]
$$\|Jg\|_{1,2;\Omega}^2\le(\ell^2+1)\|g\|_2^2+\ell^2\sum_{j=2}^d\|\partial_jg\|_2^2\le(1+\ell^2)\|g\|_{1,2;\Omega}^2.$$
All functions integrated here are smooth up to the closed box; step 1.2 licenses the iterated integrations. In dimension one the map is $Rh=Jh$, and this proves the base case. [given, F2, F5, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 1.3, step 2.1, algebra]

6.1 In dimension $d>1$, write $\Omega'=\prod_{i=2}^d(a_i,b_i)$ and $H(x')=\int_{a_1}^{b_1}h(s,x')\,ds$. Apply [F5] to this integral and each derivative identity in step 1.3, then integrate in $x'$, to obtain $$\|H\|_{1,2;\Omega'}^2\le\ell\left(\|h\|_2^2+\sum_{j=2}^d\|\partial_jh\|_2^2\right)\le\ell\|h\|_{1,2;\Omega}^2.$$ For any scalar or vector smooth $G$ on $\Omega'$, direct differentiation and separated integration give $$\|\theta_1G\|_{1,2;\Omega}^2=(\|\theta_1\|_2^2+\|\theta_1'\|_2^2)\|G\|_{2;\Omega'}^2+\|\theta_1\|_2^2\|\nabla'G\|_{2;\Omega'}^2\le B^2\|G\|_{1,2;\Omega'}^2,$$ where $B=(\|\theta_1\|_2^2+\|\theta_1'\|_2^2)^{1/2}<\infty$. Thus $g=h-\theta_1H$ satisfies $\|g\|_{1,2;\Omega}\le(1+B\sqrt\ell)\|h\|_{1,2;\Omega}$. The first component of $Rh$ is $Jg$, so step 1.4 bounds it by $\sqrt{1+\ell^2}(1+B\sqrt\ell)\|h\|_{1,2;\Omega}$. The remaining components form $\theta_1R'H$. By step 1.2, $H$ has integral zero, so the inductive estimate for the same lower-dimensional construction gives their combined norm at most $BC_{\Omega'}\sqrt\ell\|h\|_{1,2;\Omega}$. Squaring and adding the first-component and remaining-component estimates proves the claimed estimate with $$C_\Omega^2=(1+\ell^2)(1+B\sqrt\ell)^2+B^2\ell C_{\Omega'}^2.$$ This finite induction depends only on the fixed side lengths and bumps, never on the compact input support. The support, divergence and all-order test continuity properties already proved remain properties of this same map. [given, F2, F5, step 1.2, step 1.3, step 3.1, step 4.1, step 5.1, step 1.4, algebra, induction] ∎

**Given:** The hypotheses stated in the formulation, including the explicitly adopted choice principle where indicated.

[F1] [[def-axiom-of-choice]]: every family of nonempty sets has a choice function; full AC is adopted for the Sobolev completeness supplier used here.

[F2] [[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]: $W^{1,2}$ consists of $L^2$ classes with first weak derivatives in $L^2$, with the sum-of-squares Sobolev norm.

[F3] [[thm-sobolev-spaces-are-banach-spaces]]: under its stated full Axiom of Choice hypothesis, the stated $W^{1,2}$ space is complete.

[F4] [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]: a real inner product must be bilinear, symmetric and positive definite. These are axioms to verify for the displayed Sobolev pairing, not an assertion in this supplier that a particular integral pairing satisfies them.

[F5] [[def-hilbert-space]]: a real inner-product space is Hilbert when its induced norm is complete.



**Given:** Full AC, $d\ge2$, and nonempty bounded open $\Omega\subset(-R,R)^d$ with the weak-derivative convention in the Definition.

1.1 First verify the pairing on $W^{1,2}(\Omega;\mathbb R^d)$. Each coordinate of $v,w$ and each first weak derivative lies in $L^2$ by [F2]. For any two such scalar coordinates $a,b$, the pointwise inequality $2|ab|\le|a|^2+|b|^2$ proves that $ab$ is integrable. Changing either $L^2$ representative affects the product only on a null set; the weak derivative classes are unique by [F2], so the finite sum of these integrals is well-defined on the Sobolev classes. Weak differentiation is linear: adding and scaling its defining identities against every scalar test gives $\partial_j(av_i+bw_i)=a\partial_jv_i+b\partial_jw_i$, using uniqueness of weak derivatives. Linearity of integration therefore proves bilinearity of the pairing; commutativity of real multiplication proves symmetry. Finally, $$\langle v,v\rangle=\sum_i\left(\|v_i\|_2^2+\sum_j\|\partial_jv_i\|_2^2\right)=\|v\|_{W^{1,2}}^2\ge0.$$ If this is zero, every $\|v_i\|_2$ is zero, so every $v_i$ is the zero $L^2$ class and $v=0$; conversely the zero class and all its weak derivatives are zero. Thus the axioms in [F4] hold and its induced norm is exactly the displayed vector Sobolev norm. [given, F2, F3, F4, algebra]

2.1 By [F2] and [F3], each scalar component space $W^{1,2}(\Omega;\mathbb R)$ is complete under the stated AC assumption. A Cauchy sequence in the finite product $W^{1,2}(\Omega;\mathbb R^d)$ is Cauchy in each component; completeness gives a limit in each component, and the finite sum in the displayed vector norm gives convergence to the vector of those limits. Thus the vector space is complete. Its closed linear subspace $H_0^1$, defined by norm closure, is therefore complete in the inherited inner-product norm verified in step 1.1. [given, F1, F2, F3, step 1.1]

3.1 For each fixed $\phi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ the functional $v\mapsto\int_\Omega v\cdot\nabla\phi$ is continuous in the $H^1$ norm, since its absolute value is at most $\|v\|_{L^2}\|\nabla\phi\|_{L^2}$. Its kernel is closed; the intersection of these kernels is exactly $V$. Thus $V$ is a closed real linear subspace of $H_0^1$ and is complete. [given, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 The inherited pairing is positive definite and complete on $V$, so [F5] makes $V$ a real Hilbert space. The only boundary condition used is the defining closure $H_0^1$; no converse density or arbitrary-domain trace theorem has been invoked. [given, F4, F5, step 3.1] ∎
